title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One I
statement:
You are given an array `nums` in which every entry is `0` or `1`. One operation chooses three adjacent positions `i`, `i + 1` and `i + 2` and inverts each of them, so every `0` there becomes `1` and every `1` becomes `0`. You may perform any number of operations, including none.

Return the fewest operations that leave every entry of `nums` equal to `1`, or `-1` if no sequence of operations achieves that.
notes:
## Intuition

Flipping the same window twice changes nothing, and the order of flips does not matter, so an answer is just a set of window starts. Trying every set works but takes O(2ⁿ).

Look at index 0: only the window starting at 0 covers it. If `nums[0]` is 0 that window must be used, and if it is 1 it must not. Once that is settled, index 1 has only one undecided window left, the one starting at 1, so its choice is forced too, and so on along the array. Every choice is forced, so flipping exactly when the current entry is 0 while scanning left to right gives the only working set of windows, and therefore the minimum.

## Approach

1. Scan `i` from 0 while a window starting at `i` fits (`i + 2 < n`).
2. If `nums[i]` is 0, flip `nums[i]`, `nums[i + 1]` and `nums[i + 2]` in place (`^= 1` turns 0 into 1 and back) and add one to `operations`.
3. After the scan every entry before index `n - 2` is 1. The last two entries cannot start a window, so if either is still 0, return -1.
4. Otherwise return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`.

- `i = 0`: the entry is 0, so flip indices 0 to 2: `[1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0]`, `operations = 1`.
- `i = 1`: the entry is 0, so flip 1 to 3: `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]`, `operations = 2`.
- `i = 2`: the entry is 1, nothing to do.
- `i = 3`: the entry is 0, so flip 3 to 5: `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]`, `operations = 3`.

The last two entries are 1, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per index.
- Space: O(1): the flips happen inside `nums`.

## Pitfalls

- Stop the scan at index `n - 3`; a window starting later would run past the end.
- Check the last two entries afterwards: if either is 0 the answer is -1, as in Example 2 (`[0, 1, 1, 1]`).
- Never flip a window whose first entry is already 1: that entry would become 0 and no later window could repair it.
- The function changes `nums`; copy it first if the caller still needs the original.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `operations` | windows flipped so far |
| `i` | start of the window being considered; every entry before it is already 1 |

narration.2: n is the length of the array.
narration.3: No operations have been used yet.
narration.5: Consider each window start whose three positions still fit inside the array.
narration.6: Every entry before i is already 1, and only the window starting at i can still change nums[i].
narration.7: So a 0 here forces this flip: nums[i] becomes 1...
narration.9: ...and so is the one after it.
narration.13: The last two positions cannot start a window, so a 0 left there can never be fixed.
narration.16: Every entry is now 1; return the number of flips.
